CausalChain: Transient inhibition of RHOA signaling -> temporary disruption of epithelial cell polarity -> increased surface exposure of otherwise sequestered CLDN18.2 epitopes -> enhanced binding of CLDN18.2-targeted agents (e.g. antibodies, CAR-T cells) -> improved antitumor immune response
Hypothesis: Transient pharmacologic modulation of RHOA signaling in solid tumors will disrupt epithelial polarity sufficiently to unmask additional CLDN18.2 epitopes, thereby increasing the efficacy of CLDN18.2-targeted immunotherapies.
Abstract: Current research on CLDN18.2‐targeted therapies in various solid tumors, particularly gastric and gastroesophageal cancers, highlights the critical role of CLDN18.2 as a selectively expressed antigen on tumor cells. Studies indicate that the disruption of cell polarity during malignant transformation leads to the exposure of CLDN18.2 epitopes that are otherwise sequestered in tight junctions. Nevertheless, in certain tumors the limited surface availability of CLDN18.2 may contribute to suboptimal responses to targeted agents. Here, we propose that transient modulation of epithelial cell polarity via controlled inhibition of RHOA signaling may unmask additional CLDN18.2 epitopes, thereby enhancing the binding and efficacy of CLDN18.2‐directed immunotherapies such as monoclonal antibodies, bispecific constructs, and CAR‑T cells. This strategy, by temporarily altering the tumor microenvironment and epithelial integrity, could improve therapeutic response in tumors with otherwise low CLDN18.2 accessibility.
